* Port the material model and its store to Dart

Jokes, sets, shows and the library that resolves a set's ids back into
jokes, plus the file store that carries them between launches.

The port's real risk is a value quietly becoming a default, so the
unknown states are what the tests are built around: an unestimated joke
contributes nothing to a set's planned length rather than a guess, an
unknown audience size stays distinct from an empty room across a round
trip, and a descriptor an older build does not recognise decodes to
unknown rather than to the first option of its enum. Confirmed each by
mutation: guessing 60s, and decoding to values.first, both go red.

The store writes aside and renames rather than writing in place. Losing
material to a kill on stage is the one unforgivable bug, and a rename
within a directory is atomic where a partial write is not.

Ids are generated here rather than taken from a package — a v4 UUID is
a few lines, and it is the only thing the product would use one for.

Refs #40

* Port the stage state machine to Dart

The queued/live/told machine behind the card taps, and the segments they
open and close. Tapping a queued card closes the live segment and opens
the next at the same instant, so no gap belongs to neither bit; tapping
the live card is ignored rather than opening a zero-length segment; and
tapping a told card re-opens it while leaving its first segment intact,
which is what the callback in the mockups does.

The started tally counts distinct jokes, not segments, so a bit returned
to still counts once. Mutation-checked, along with the ignored re-tap
and the manual provenance every tap records.

The segment-mode switch throws rather than staying quietly off. A
control that reads "on" while nothing detects would lie on stage.

Refs #40

* Port the review analytics to Dart

The countdown's tone thresholds and the take-anomaly rule.

Both refusals in the anomaly rule are the substance: fewer than three
comparison takes is no norm, and zero spread among them is no signal
rather than an infinitely strong one. Each returns unknown, never a zero
deviation, so a caller cannot mistake "cannot say" for "not anomalous".

The first version of the fewer-than-three test passed for the wrong
reason — its two comparison takes were identical, so the zero-sigma
refusal answered before the count was ever consulted, and lowering the
threshold to two did not red it. It now uses takes with real spread, and
a companion test adds only a third take to pin the boundary.

Refs #40

* Detect laughs from the recording's loudness envelope

The first code in the conversion that is not a port. Decision D7: in a
club, sustained room noise above the room's own level is laughter, and
the product does not need to tell laughter from applause from cheering.
So detection is RMS per frame, a threshold relative to a low quantile of
those frames, and a minimum duration — a pure function of the samples,
with no model, no clock and no I/O, which is what lets requirement 6.9
promise identical events on every platform and every run.

Two choices carry the weight, and both are pinned by a test that fails
when they are reversed:

The baseline is a low quantile, not the mean. On a set that storms,
laughter occupies most of the recording and drags the mean up until the
threshold sits above the laughter itself — the better the set went, the
fewer laughs it would find. Swapping in the mean takes that test from
four events to zero.

Intensity is absolute rather than normalised against the recording's own
peak. Were it relative, every show's best laugh would read 1.0 and takes
from different rooms could not be compared, which is what keeping takes
is for.

The settings live in one named object rather than as defaults spread
through the detector: they are a calibration, and one nobody can point
at is one nobody can review. They are provisional — checked against
synthesised signals only, never against club audio, which is risk R1 and
a Phase B step. The synthetic fixture says so at the point it is built.

Refs #40

* Widen the recording seam and port the capture coordinator

The whole platform surface of the product, and the reason the port is
cheap: with nothing analysing during capture (D8), neither platform has
to hand raw audio to Dart, so what crosses is commands down and small
events up.

The Swift protocol it replaces carried only start, stop, captured and
isRunning — no way for the platform to report a level for the stage
strip, and no way to say the microphone had been taken. Both were
needed, so the seam now carries an event stream: a level to draw, and
interruption transitions. It carries no way to pass samples across at
all, which is requirement 6.7 made structural rather than promised.

The coordinator keeps one file per uninterrupted stretch and a clock
that counts recorded audio rather than wall time, so a stamp indexes
into the audio and never rewinds across a gap.

Starting a part now takes the show as an argument instead of reading the
field, because both callers had already established it and the second
check inside made the first one dead. Mutation-testing is what surfaced
it: deleting either guard changed no behaviour and no test. Removing it
now fails to compile.

* Scaffold the Flutter workspace and pin the SDK

Two packages, split by what may touch a platform: setlist_core is pure
Dart and forbidden from importing Flutter, so the stage machine, the
timeline and detection behave identically everywhere; setlist_ui holds
the screens.

They sit beside the Swift tree rather than replacing it. Both are live
until the Swift one is deleted, so main stays green throughout.

The SDK version is pinned in .flutter-version rather than tracking
stable. A renderer change re-rasterises text and moves every golden at
once, which reads as the whole screen kind regressing rather than as a
toolchain bump (risk R6). The lockfiles are committed for the same
reason: a floating dependency can move a render too.

Refs #40

* Port the capture timeline to Dart

The first slice of the core, chosen because it carries the rule most
easily lost in a port: taps and laughs share one monotonic clock, and at
an equal stamp the tap comes first. A laugh is filed under the bit that
was live when it happened, so inverting that tie-break moves a bit's
opening laugh onto the bit before it. Watched the test catch exactly
that, by inverting the comparator.

LaughEvent lands in its post-conversion shape: start, duration and
intensity, with no class, confidence or detector id (requirement 6.3).

Refs #40

* Bundle the product's fonts so goldens can see text

A Flutter test renders text in a glyph-less stub font by default, where
every character is the same filled box. Measured on this toolchain
before fixing it: THE STAND and THE STANE rendered byte-identically,
while a length change produced a 17976px diff. So a golden catches
layout and silently accepts wrong copy of the same length — and this
spec pins exact strings at more than a dozen leaves.

The families are read from the bundle's own FontManifest, so the
harness renders with whatever the product ships and the two cannot
drift apart by editing one of them. DejaVu covers the punctuation the
copy leans on: the middle dot in 2.3, the true minus sign in 2.5, the
tilde in 4.5.

The committed test is the assurance, not a demonstration: it renders two
strings that differ by one character and nothing else and requires the
pixels to differ. Watched it fail with the fonts unloaded, with the
message it exists to print.

Refs #40

* Run the Dart packages in CI

A fourth lane on ubuntu, beside the Swift ones rather than replacing
them. It resolves the SDK from .flutter-version so CI renders with the
version the goldens were approved under.

Unverified against a real run: Actions has assigned no runner to this
repository since 2026-08-21, so no workflow has executed (#44).

* Author the Phase A executable spec

Forty-two numbered leaves for the client-only MVP, seeded from the owner's
screen-level requirements and the mockups: library, stage mode (rendered and
driven), capture, review, and the consent/privacy surface App Review reads.

Refs #6

* Make the spec executable: coverage gate, harness, and the core it proves

The gate is the bijection: every leaf is claimed by exactly one case of a
registered kind, or is a tracked gap in pending.json with its reason. It also
generates each kind's Swift manifest (Swift discovers no case file at runtime)
and the spec's golden gallery, and checks both byte-for-byte.

Seventeen leaves land claimed by logic cases against SetlistCore — the material
model, the stage state machine behind card taps, the capture clock both taps and
laugh events are stamped on, the countdown and anomaly rules. The other
twenty-five are specified and marked TBD: the screen kind needs a simulator lane
that does not exist yet, and the capture leaves need a device or a faithful
audio-session fake.

Refs #6

* Build the app shell and its CI lanes

Three jobs: the coverage gate on Node, the requirement cases in a Swift
container, and the iPad app built from the XcodeGen spec on macOS. Agent
sessions here have no Swift toolchain and no macOS, so the Swift half of every
change is verified by these checks rather than locally.

Refs #6

* Give each kind's manifest a unique basename

One module compiles all three, and same-basename sources collide on their
object file — the Swift lane could not build. The gate names them after their
kind and the README leaves the target's sources.

Refs #6

* Close five spec gaps: the library store and capture leaves are provable

1.6, 3.4, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.6 leave the burn-down list. The capture three name
their boundary in the doc: they confirm the app asks for a recording of the
right shape, not that the platform delivers one — 4.5 stays a gap because no
fake can stand in for a locked screen.

Refs #6

* Add the library store and the capture coordinator

Sets now reference their jokes by id, so a joke edited in the library is edited
on every set list that plans it, and a set naming a deleted joke is shorter
rather than broken. The library round-trips through a file in the app's
container, written atomically — material lost to a kill on stage is the one
unforgivable bug.

The capture coordinator owns when the recording runs, where it goes, and the
clock card taps and laugh events share. An interruption closes the stretch so
far and resumes into the same show; the clock counts recorded seconds, so a
stamp indexes into the audio and never rewinds across the gap.

Refs #6

* Render the stage screen, and make a screen requirement executable

The stage screen from the mockups, as SwiftUI over the same StageModel the
driven cases use: header with the recording indicator and countdown, pacing bar
weighted by each bit's estimate, the current joke with its setups highlighted,
the laugh strip, the segment-mode switch, and the 3x3 grid coloured told/live/
queued.

The screen kind renders a real view at one portrait iPad screen and compares it
pixel for pixel with a committed golden — no tolerance, because a tolerance is
an invitation for unreviewed drift. It runs on the simulator, so its manifest is
empty off Apple platforms and the macOS lane is what executes it. 2.5 claims the
first case and is red until its render is approved: the refresh-goldens workflow
is the only thing that writes a golden.

Refs #6

* Give the refresh workflow a bash default so a failing pipe fails the step

Refs #6

* Ten screen leaves become executable; the switch records why it cannot

Nine stage-mode leaves leave the burn-down list beside 2.5. 2.12 stays, with
the reason at the leaf: the renderer refuses to flatten a UIKit-backed control,
and a SwiftUI lookalike would pass the golden while breaking the requirement.

Refs #6

* Claim the stage screen's rendered states

Each leaf renders the real StageScreen over one shared fixture — the mockup's
nine bits, three told, one live — so goldens differ only where the requirement
differs. Every one is red until its render is approved through the refresh
workflow.

Refs #6

* Let a branch trigger a golden refresh [refresh goldens]

workflow_dispatch is only offered for workflows already on the default branch,
so the branch that adds a screen case could not ask for its render. A commit
message marker gives it a way in.

Refs #6

xcodebuild does not carry an environment variable into a hostless test bundle's
process, so the refresh run compared against goldens that do not exist yet
instead of writing them. The marker is a file the workflow drops beside the
cases for one run.

* Refresh screen goldens, re-rendered by the refresh-goldens workflow

* Fill the screen, count the live joke, and highlight setups visibly [refresh goldens]

Three defects the first render showed. The set list sized to its text and left
the bottom third of the iPad empty; it now takes whatever the joke panel does
not. The live joke read 0:00 because a card's run time counted only closed
segments, so the model now answers run time as of a moment. And the setup
highlight was drawn in the panel's own dark ink, which reads as de-emphasis —
exactly backwards for the words the punch depends on.

A runner image that ships a new iOS runtime re-renders every golden, which

Refs #6

* Reshape the spec to the form the other two projects use

Compared against EdFringeNow's product/requirements.md and ShoutsAndWhispers'
dev/requirements/requirements.md, ours was coarse: fourteen broad leaves for a
whole screen, no copy pinned anywhere, and one moment rendered ten times. Both
references read as a spine of one-line claims with the visible strings quoted
verbatim, and cover a screen's states rather than one of them.

So the stage screen becomes four sections — header, current joke, set list,
segmenting — with the exact copy the mockups specify quoted at the leaf, and
its states separated: the countdown neutral, warning and over; the laugh strip
lit and dim; the set before anything is tapped. A fixture-world paragraph names
the moment every render draws, and the notes fold into details blocks so the
document reads as its numbered spine.

Section 9 adds sagas, the kind we were missing: a story told as one captioned
frame per step, which is the only way to state what a card tap changes.

Leaves are renumbered, which the framework forbids once ids are in use — doing
it here, before anything has merged and while the only reader is the open PR,
is the last moment it is free.

Refs #6

Twenty screen cases over five distinct fixture states, and the first saga:
six captioned frames of a set being worked — the opener going up, the set
moving on, the callback taking the comedian back to a bit already told, and
the slot running out underneath them.

A saga's frames are ..step-NN.png beside its case, with the captions
generated next to them: a caption list hand-maintained in Markdown drifts from
the frames it labels, and the gate now fails when their counts disagree. The
gallery generator learned to lay a captioned strip out under a leaf, and to
converge — the blank line before a block is part of the block, or regeneration
grows one blank per run and never reaches a fixed point.

Refs #6

* Refresh screen goldens, re-rendered by the refresh-goldens workflow

* Give every fixture bit a real body [refresh goldens]

The saga's frames put jokes other than Airport security on stage, and eight of
the nine had an ellipsis where the words go — so the frame that proves the
callback return read as a broken screen rather than a comedian mid-bit. The
gallery is where the owner reviews the product, so its fixture has to look like
the product.

Refs #6

* Refresh screen goldens, re-rendered by the refresh-goldens workflow

* Drop the placeholder holding the behavior kind open

It has five cases now.

Refs #6

* Crop every screen golden to the element its leaf is about [refresh goldens]

A requirement about the countdown was being proved by a picture of the whole
iPad, and so were sixteen others — which makes reviewing a spec mean re-reading
one screen twenty times to find the thing each line claims.

The screen now publishes its own named regions, and a case asks for the one its
leaf is about; the golden is that region cropped out of a full render of the
composed screen. Always out of the composed screen — laying an element out
alone would prove it in a context the product never shows. Three leaves keep the
whole screen and say why at the leaf: two claim something about the screen
itself, and one compares the joke panel against everything around it, which a
crop of the panel cannot do.

Refs #6

* Let a region contain the regions inside it [refresh goldens]

Publishing a region with anchorPreference replaces whatever the view's children
published, so the current-joke panel erased the title row, the body, the tags
and the laugh strip — five leaves could not find the element they are about.
Transforming the preference merges instead.

Refs #6

* Refresh screen goldens, re-rendered by the refresh-goldens workflow

* Make a screen case declare what it captures

A picture of the whole screen where the leaf is about one element still passes
— it just proves less, which is invisible in a green run. So the gate requires
every screen case to either name its region or say, at the case, why the whole
screen is the proof. Watched it fire on a case with its region removed.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Both reviewed properly — I ran them rather than read them.

**[#70](https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/pull/70) — correct, merge it.** One file, six lines. Its claim checks out structurally (`dev/requirements/` has no `test/` directory; `runner_test.dart` sits at the package root), and independently: `ci.yml:69` runs exactly `flutter test runner_test.dart` there. So CI has always used the working command while the rule I wrote told humans the broken one.

**[#68](https://github.com/missingbulb/WIP/pull/68) — sound, merge it.** I verified it the hard way: injected a real violation into `stage_fits_test.dart` and ran the full world sweep. It fires at the right line, blocking, exit 1, with a useful message; clean tree gives exit 0. Fixture 3/3.

Getting there took a wrong turn worth reporting, because it nearly became a false accusation:

> My first injection produced **zero findings**, and I was ready to call the check broken. It wasn't. `enclosedBy` matches by **indentation**, not braces — it walks up for the first *less-indented* line and requires that to be the opener. My Python injection landed `await loadProductFonts();` at the same indent as `testWidgets(`, so the matcher stepped straight over it. Real code — anything `dart format` has touched — is properly nested. **My test was malformed, not the check.**

That does expose a genuine, minor limit: the matcher is indentation-based, so a mis-indented violation escapes. In a formatted Dart repo that's near-theoretical, and it's a property of the shared engine, not this PR.

Two things I'd note without blocking:

**The prose deletion loses one diagnostic.** The old bullet said the failure "presents as the second test in a file being slow, not as an error" — the clue that cost me a long time to find. The check's message helps whoever *writes* the bad line, but a hang arriving by another route (a helper function calling `loadProductFonts`) fires nothing and the hint is gone.

**The fixture proves the pattern, not the wiring.** It calls `loadDeclaredChecks(PACK_DIR)` directly, bypassing the sweep's pack discovery. That's exactly the trap the repo's own rule warns about — a synthetic fixture can only confirm the matching. The real-tree run I did is the part that actually proves it, and it passed.

Together they merge cleanly in either order despite overlapping hunks in `RULES.md`, and the combined tree is green:

```
merged sweep exit=0     fixture 3/3 pass     no conflicts either direction
```

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent

4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.

   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if

7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
